newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia set for growth, dep minister warns on debt.
newsitem.headline: Russia set for growth, dep minister warns on debt.

text.p: Russia's economy is on track for growth in 1997, top Russian finance officials said on Wednesday, but a deputy minister warned of a looming crisis over the cost of servicing domestic debt.

Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said gross domestic product was likely to grow in 1997 despite a budget which was "less reformist but better practical policy" than earlier government spending plans.

"It is clear that we have a chance of achieving two percent growth," Livshits told a meeting of financiers. Output in the first 11 months of this year was six percent less than in the corresponding period of 1995.
Livshits promised to improve the tax system and the military next year but added "No reforms are free."

The State Duma lower house of parliament in a first reading on Sunday approved a compromise budget for 1997. It envisaged a deficit of 3.5 percent of GDP. The government had originally proposed a gap of 3.3 percent.
Central bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin said Russia's tight monetary policy had paid off with low inflation, which had slowed to about 24 percent this year from 131 percent in 1995.
He predicted it would slow to 10-12 percent in 1997 and said that as a result Russians were more ready to use the rouble, even though prices are still often marked in dollars.
"We have achieved confidence in the rouble," he said, adding that the bank would increase M2 money supply by about 35 percent in 1997, faster than prices would rise.
Dubinin said high yields on rouble instruments were in line with a plan to de-dollarise the economy.
Dollars, barter, and monetary surrogates such as promissory notes issued by enterprises have marginalised the rouble in some regions where there is a cash shortage.
"Our goal is de-dollarisation and our stimulus is more profitable uses for roubles than for foreign currency," Dubinin said.
But a deputy finance minister told the same conference that Russia might not be able to raise enough money to service its growing domestic debt by the end of 1998.
"The government is moving towards a situation where internal savings are not enough to cover internal debt," said Oleg Vyugin.
Government securities yield about 40 percent, and Dubinin predicted the yield would fall by half to about four to five percentage points above the rate of inflation by the end of 1997.
But tax revenues from Russian companies, even under the government's growth scenario, would grow slower than the government's debt service payment schedule, Vyugin said.
So long as the rate of economic growth was outstripped by yields on government securities, the government would always be scraping for money and at the mercy of the market, he concluded.

"The availability of modest financial reserves in regard to work on financial markets allows one quickly to reduce interest rates and, on the other hand, absence of reserves allows market participants to force up interest rates, even if they are excessively high," he said.
